items.title: S&P set for record open as a Hormuz 'deal' story does the Fed's job for it

Gold is up ~1%, Bitcoin flat, STOXX 600 +0.6%, Kospi +1.6%.
items.angle: Oil down 4% on a 'deal' that hasn't been signed is the cheapest volatility purchase in the market right now — a cheap downside hedge if Hormuz talk stalls again like every prior round this year.
items.tweetA: Oil -4% on a Hormuz 'deal' that isn't signed yet. We've been here at least three times this year. The options market is pricing this headline as fact — the crude puts nobody wants are the cheap hedge.
items.tweetB: S&P record highs financed by a 2bp move in the 10Y and a phone call about Hormuz. That's not a re-rating, that's a headline doing the Fed's job for a day. $USO $SPX

items.tweetA: Treasury Secretary talks the 10Y down 2bps. The 30Y — the part he doesn't control — doesn't move an inch. That gap between belly and long end IS the market's vote on Fed credibility right now.
items.tweetB: 3 FOMC members dissented FOR a hike last month. Market-implied path moved from cuts to net tightening. And equities are at records. Someone's wrong between now and Friday's payroll. $TLT $SPX

items.title: Biggest week of retail selling since 2022, and Asia hedge funds just had their worst month on record
items.idea: Citadel Securities clocked two of the three largest retail tech-selling days on record last week, Goldman prime says Asia hedge funds had their worst month ever, and Russell 3000 short interest sits near a multi-year high of 2.9% of market cap — the melt-up looks like a positioning unwind, not new conviction.
items.angle: This is the fuel bulls are pointing to, but washed-out positioning explains the bounce's speed, not its durability — watch whether volume follows price once the shorts are covered.
items.tweetA: Worst month on record for Asia hedge funds. Two of the three largest retail tech-selling days ever, last week. And somehow that's the bull case for new highs — because everyone who wanted to sell already did.
items.tweetB: 2.9% short interest on the Russell 3000, a multi-year high, walking straight into a rally. Every squeeze needs fuel — the question nobody's asking is what happens after the shorts are gone.

items.title: A startup wants to route AI's intercontinental data through space lasers instead of the ocean floor
items.idea: 95% of intercontinental data still crosses roughly 500 subsea cables that take up to a decade to build and are increasingly getting cut (Red Sea 2024, repeatedly near Taiwan) with zero accountability; Endeavor Optical Networks is betting laser links between satellites and ground stations can bypass the chokepoint entirely, offering route-diverse bandwidth that never touches the seabed.
items.angle: If undersea cables are now a target in great-power conflict, laser-relay bandwidth is a defense-tech and AI-infra story at once — the kind of dual-use infrastructure play that can pull DoD and hyperscaler money simultaneously.
items.tweetA: 500 cables carry 95% of the world's intercontinental data. Multiple have been cut near Taiwan with zero consequences. A space-laser network sounds like sci-fi until you realize it's the only redundancy a fishing trawler can't cut.
items.tweetB: Hyperscalers now own the majority of new subsea cable capacity because leasing got too slow. That's the same logic that will make them the first customers for orbital laser relays — control the pipe or starve.

items.title: Russia's most influential living strategist just gave a masterclass in why the sea is the next front
items.idea: Patrushev, the former FSB director who remains one of the Kremlin's top strategic minds, frames the next confrontation with the West around maritime power — relevant given roughly 80% of world trade by volume moves by sea and undersea cables/pipelines sit largely undefended.
items.angle: Britain is already debating Royal Navy overstretch; combine this with the a16z cable-cutting story above and you get the same thesis from two unrelated sources — maritime chokepoints are becoming the preferred arena for grey-zone escalation.
items.tweetA: 80% of world trade by volume moves by sea. Russia's most influential living strategist is talking openly about maritime confrontation. Meanwhile the Royal Navy is stretched thin and nobody's guarding the cables. This is the theater nobody's pricing.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching Ukraine's front lines. Patrushev is talking about the ocean floor. Two unrelated newsletters, same week, same conclusion: the next escalation isn't on land.

items.title: An FBI counterintelligence agent stole $1M from the crypto wallets he was investigating — targets tied to Russia
items.idea: Patrick Yaroch pulled seed phrases from bureau systems 10-12 times since late 2024, moved roughly $1M, then confessed on Signal saying the theft was 'eating him up inside' — two sources say the targeted accounts were Russia-linked, and he had booked flights to Portugal with power-of-attorney documents ready and ChatGPT chats about leaving the US with the money.
items.angle: This is a live operational-security failure inside the agency that's supposed to be the last line of defense on crypto-enabled sanctions evasion — worth watching what internal controls get rewritten.
items.tweetA: An FBI counterintelligence agent had the keys to Russia-linked wallets his own bureau was investigating — and helped himself. If seed phrases sit on internal systems that accessible, the custody problem isn't retail, it's the agency guarding the wallets.
items.tweetB: He confessed because guilt ate him alive, not because he got caught. Which means the systems that were supposed to catch this didn't. Ask what else hasn't confessed yet.

items.title: Coldcard's 2021 firmware bug just became a $130M hardware-wallet breach — and 90% of the stolen BTC hasn't moved
items.idea: Galaxy Research has confirmed 1,596 BTC (over $100M) drained across three waves from roughly 7,300 addresses, with a suspected fourth wave that would push the total to 2,055 BTC (about $130M); the root cause is a March 2021 firmware error that made seeds guessable, and a fixed firmware doesn't repair a seed already generated.
items.angle: This is the first self-custody breach at real scale — the 'not your keys, not your coins' crowd just learned hardware wallets carry supply-chain risk too, and 90% of stolen coins sitting unmoved means the thief is patient, not panicked.
items.tweetA: $130M drained from a hardware wallet bug that shipped in 2021 and went uncaught for five years. 'Cold storage is safe' just took its biggest hit since Mt. Gox. The seed was compromised at birth — no firmware patch un-generates a bad key.
items.tweetB: 90% of the stolen Coldcard bitcoin hasn't moved. That's not a smash-and-grab, that's someone sitting on a $100M+ position waiting for the noise to die down. Watch those addresses.

items.title: Saylor is now selling Bitcoin at an $11,462-per-coin loss to keep his own preferred stock alive
items.idea: Strategy sold 1,638 BTC at $63,957 (vs. a $75,419 cost basis) to fund $52.4M in preferred dividends and an $81M STRC buyback — STRC has traded below its $100 par since mid-May, and this is Strategy's longest pause on BTC buying ever (5+ weeks).
items.angle: The 'never sell' pledge just quietly became 'sell to prop up the structure that was supposed to let us never sell' — the tell that the MSTR/STRC flywheel now needs external cash to keep spinning, not just BTC appreciation.
items.tweetA: Saylor built an empire on 'never sell your Bitcoin.' Today he's selling Bitcoin at an $11,462/coin loss to buy back his own preferred stock. The kidney joke just became balance-sheet reality.
items.tweetB: STRC's been under par since May. Strategy hasn't bought BTC in 5+ weeks — its longest pause ever. When the machine built to buy Bitcoin forever starts selling to fund its own preferred, that's not a treasury strategy anymore, it's liability management.

items.title: Tony Greer: 'The idea of hodling is completely absurd now that MicroStrategy is a net seller'
items.idea: Greer is short semis and SpaceX on the view the market 'can't have it both ways' — a semiconductor bubble expanding into the stratosphere while a $2T SpaceX valuation and Google's $80B raise get absorbed simultaneously — and flags that every 2025 'Trump trade' (Bitcoin, Coinbase, uranium, rare earths, solar) got 'shot in the back' as Trump's approval fell.
items.angle: The SpaceX-semis pair trade is a bet that AI-capex enthusiasm and pre-IPO mega-valuations can't both be right at once — worth tracking against actual SpaceX funding-round pricing as it firms up.
items.tweetA: Tony Greer's logic: you can't price a semiconductor bubble AND land a $2T SpaceX valuation AND have Google raise $80B, all in the same breath. Something in that stack gives first, and he's betting it's semis.
items.tweetB: Every 'Trump trade' from early 2026 — Bitcoin, Coinbase, uranium, rare earths, solar — is now underwater as his approval slides. If policy trades tracked the President's polling that closely on the way up, they'll track it on the way down too.

items.title: The entire quality-investing playbook in one equation: Growth = ROIC × Reinvestment Rate
items.idea: A company earning 25% ROIC reinvesting 40% of profit compounds at 10%; a company earning 10% ROIC reinvesting 65% compounds at only 6.5% despite plowing back far more capital — reinvestment rate without high ROIC is capital destruction at a slower pace.
items.angle: Screen for ROIC above 15% first, reinvestment rate second — most retail growth screens do it backwards, ranking on growth rate alone without decomposing where the growth actually comes from.
items.tweetA: Company A reinvests 40% of profit at 25% ROIC. Company B reinvests 65% at 10% ROIC. B is 'trying harder' and still compounds slower. Reinvestment rate is a multiplier on quality, not a substitute for it.
items.tweetB: Every growth screen ranks on revenue growth. None of them ask whether that growth was bought with 25% ROIC capital or 10% ROIC capital. That's the entire difference between a compounder and a value trap.

items.title: Diploma PLC: buying 6-8x-earnings distributors and raising prices 3-5% a year because customers never notice
items.idea: Diploma consolidates niche industrial/aerospace/medical parts distributors — products that are mission-critical (a bolt for a 787, a sterile MRI valve) but represent just 0.2% of the customer's total costs — and has compounded at 18.9% annually for 34 years buying founder-run businesses at 6-8x earnings and leaving them alone.
items.angle: The 0.2%-of-costs detail is the actual moat: pricing power exists exactly where the line item is too small for anyone to fight over — a repeatable playbook across any fragmented, mission-critical, low-relative-cost category.
items.tweetA: 0.2% of total costs. That's Diploma's whole moat — sell something so mission-critical and so cheap relative to what it protects that nobody ever pushes back on a price increase. 34 years, 18.9% annual returns, buying tiny distributors at 6-8x earnings.
items.tweetB: Everyone hunts for pricing power in branded consumer goods. The better hunting ground is industrial bolts and MRI valves — anything critical enough to never get substituted and cheap enough to never get negotiated.

items.title: The Coinbase BTC Premium Index just logged its longest negative streak ever — 78 days of missing US retail demand
items.idea: Bitcoin has absorbed the Coldcard hack and Saylor's own selling this week and is still roughly flat, but the Coinbase premium (a proxy for US retail buy pressure vs. offshore) has been negative for 78 straight days, the longest streak on record.
items.angle: Flat price despite terrible news plus a record-long retail-demand drought is either a market that's already de-risked, or a sign that whoever's holding the bid isn't retail at all — worth checking against ETF flow data.
items.tweetA: 78 days of negative Coinbase premium — the longest streak ever — while BTC shrugs off a $130M hack and its biggest corporate holder selling at a loss. Either retail is done capitulating or retail was never the bid to begin with.
items.tweetB: Bad news stopped moving the price this week. That's usually called 'exhaustion' at the bottom of a cycle or 'someone bigger than retail is absorbing everything' near the top of one. The premium data rules out retail either way.

items.title: BlackRock put tokenized money market funds on Solana and Ethereum in the same week Solana's fee burn is set to 14x
items.idea: BlackRock's new tokenized MMFs record ownership onchain via Securitize while holding only cash and short-term Treasurys — a stablecoin-reserve vehicle — landing the same week Solana's fee-burn proposal (raising daily burns from roughly $47K to $646K equivalent) went to an initial vote.
items.angle: BlackRock choosing Solana as a settlement rail for a TradFi product, not just Ethereum, is the tell that Solana's institutional case has moved past 'meme coin casino' in allocators' heads.
items.tweetA: BlackRock didn't just tokenize a money market fund — it put one on Solana. Six months ago that sentence would have gotten laughed out of an IC meeting.
items.tweetB: Solana's fee burn is about to 14x (from ~$47K/day to ~$646K/day) the same week BlackRock shows up as a settlement venue. Supply mechanics and institutional adoption moving the same direction rarely stays quiet for long. $SOL

items.title: WSJ: $7 trillion in AI data center capex over 4 years is enough to damage the economy on its own
items.idea: The Journal's framing, quoted approvingly by Rosenberg, is that the AI buildout doesn't need to be a bubble that pops to hurt the economy — capital misallocation on that scale, increasingly debt-financed, can drag growth even if productivity gains eventually show up, and the debt-financing angle means a disappointment hits the financial system too.
items.angle: This reframes the AI-bubble debate away from 'will it pay off' toward 'can the economy absorb the spending regardless of the answer' — a much harder question to dismiss with an ROIC argument alone.
items.tweetA: $7 trillion in data center capex over 4 years. Even if AI eventually pays for itself, that's enough capital misallocation to dent GDP on the way there. The bubble/no-bubble debate is a distraction from the pace-of-spending problem.
items.tweetB: The AI capex debate keeps asking 'will the returns show up.' The better question: does the debt financing behind that $7T care whether the returns show up on time? Financial systems don't get a grace period for productivity to catch up.

items.title: A quant signal service just admitted BTC is in 'no man's land' — no new trades in weeks
items.idea: No new signals have fired in the model for a couple of weeks as Bitcoin consolidates in a range the author explicitly calls untradeable territory for his system.
items.angle: A systematic model going silent for weeks is itself a data point — realized-vol and momentum inputs have compressed enough that no rules-based signal is firing, consistent with the Lucky Trader item above on BTC's flat price action despite bad news.
items.tweetA: A quant model going silent for two weeks isn't 'no news' — it's the model telling you volatility and momentum have both compressed below its trigger threshold. Combine that with the Coinbase premium data and BTC's chart is genuinely asleep right now.
items.tweetB: No man's land is a fine place for a trend-follower to sit out. It's a terrible place for anyone underwriting a directional thesis on either side.

items.title: Global liquidity momentum is slowing even as levels hold — and the rotation is out of Asia tech into Europe

items.tweetA: Liquidity momentum is rolling over globally, but nobody's de-risking — they're just moving the risk from Asia tech to Europe. That's not risk-off, that's a rotation trade hiding inside a flat headline number.
items.tweetB: Soft dollar + stable collateral + slowing CB liquidity = risk-on can persist even as the fuel runs low. Watch what breaks first once the dollar stops cooperating.

items.title: Boockvar: the yen rescue is fleeting unless the BoJ actually hikes in September — JGB 2yr just hit a 31-year high
items.idea: September BoJ hike odds jumped to roughly 50% from 27% right before last week's intervention, the JGB 2yr yield is at a fresh 31-year high and the 10yr is 2bps from a 29-year high — and Japan used the Fed's FIMA repo facility to fund the intervention, money that has to be paid back from somewhere.
items.angle: The FIMA repo detail is the underrated risk: an intervention funded by a facility that requires repayment creates a second, delayed source of selling pressure down the road, separate from whatever the BoJ decides in September.
items.tweetA: Japan intervened using the Fed's own repo facility. That money doesn't just appear — it has to be paid back. Everyone's watching the yen level; the real risk is what gets sold later to fund the payback.
items.tweetB: BoJ hike odds for September: 27% a week ago, ~50% now. JGB 2yr at a 31-year high. The bond market is doing what the intervention couldn't — pricing the actual policy response before the meeting even happens.

items.title: Boockvar's earnings scorecard: Boise Cascade says housing is 'subdued,' Whirlpool blames tariffs for margin pressure
items.idea: Boise Cascade flags affordability constraints and weak consumer sentiment pressuring new-construction demand despite homebuilder incentives, while Whirlpool's North America EBIT margin fell y/y on the 'unfavorable impact of tariff, raw material inflation and fuel costs' even as pricing actions drove an 8% sequential sales gain.
items.angle: Two unrelated industrials both naming tariffs and rates as the same drag in the same earnings season is a cleaner read on 'uneven economy' than any single data print — worth tracking against Friday's payrolls for confirmation.
items.tweetA: Boise Cascade: housing demand needs homebuilder incentives just to move. Whirlpool: tariffs are eating the margin gains from price hikes. Two unrelated companies, same earnings season, same two culprits — rates and tariffs. That's not noise, that's a macro read.
items.tweetB: Whirlpool raised prices 8% sequentially and still lost margin to tariffs and input costs. Pricing power isn't enough when the cost side inflates faster than you can pass it through.

items.title: Factor volatility hit an all-time high in July. Bitcoin's volatility hit a cycle low. Same month.
items.idea: AI momentum-factor volatility exploded past levels seen in the dot-com bubble and GFC while Bitcoin's 365-day realized vol ended July at 37% (near multi-year lows) despite absorbing a double-digit drawdown that would historically have pushed vol past 60-80%. The thesis: AI is compressing 'moat duration' (the author's 'Intelligence Competition Paradox') faster than DCFs can reprice it, while Bitcoin has no moat to defend and is therefore immune to the same repricing.
items.angle: This is the sharpest 'why is Bitcoin quiet while AI stocks are violent' framework circulating right now — the trade implication is own physical bottlenecks plus distribution/trust layers plus scarcity assets, and underweight anything whose valuation depends on a moat AI can erode in a quarter.
items.tweetA: Bitcoin's realized vol: 37%, near a multi-year low, after absorbing a double-digit drawdown. AI-stock factor vol: above dot-com and GFC levels. The asset with zero cash flows is now the calm one in the room. Sit with that for a second.
items.tweetB: Every AI moat that took a decade to build can now get pressured in a quarter — Kimi K3 proved frontier capability spreads in days, not years. The market isn't repricing AI winners because they're losing. It's repricing them because 'winning' stopped meaning anything durable.

items.title: Six AI/semiconductor ETFs now account for 19% of all US ETF trading volume
items.idea: Leveraged and inverse ETF exposure has fallen since June but trading activity and speculative inflows remain elevated, and daily rebalancing means these products can lose value even if the underlying index round-trips back to where it started — mechanical flows are now dictating market speed and route, not just direction.
items.angle: This explains a lot of the intraday whipsaw in AI names that doesn't map cleanly to news flow — check options/ETF rebalancing windows into the close before assuming a move is fundamentally driven.
items.tweetA: 6 ETFs = 19% of all US ETF volume, all AI/semis. When a sector's daily flow is dominated by mechanical rebalancing, the 'why did it move' question stops being about earnings and starts being about 3:45pm rebalance flow.
items.tweetB: Leveraged ETFs can lose money even if the index they track ends up exactly where it started. Daily rebalancing decay isn't a disclaimer footnote anymore — it's 19% of market volume.

items.title: Greece just used a shipping tycoon to kill an EU sanctions package — and Brussels' fix is to end the veto that let it happen
items.idea: Greece held up the EU's latest Russia sanctions package to protect a domestic shipping tycoon, and the European Commission's response is to start passing sanctions in small thematic batches specifically to reduce members' ability to invoke vetoes — the same veto power that was sold as the 'ultimate backstop' justifying EU membership in the first place.
items.angle: This connects directly to a winter gas crunch call — if unanimity is being engineered away right when member-state energy interests diverge most, that's the moment national capitals either accept a weaker veto or start actively resisting Brussels.
items.tweetA: The EU was sold on an inviolable member veto. Twenty-plus sanctions packages later, Brussels' fix for a veto used to protect a shipping tycoon is... removing the veto. The bait-and-switch just got explicit.
items.tweetB: Watch what happens to unanimity requirements right as winter gas math gets ugly. An EU that engineers away vetoes when energy interests diverge is an EU testing how much sovereignty it can quietly delete before someone actually leaves.

items.title: Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max: a 2.4 trillion parameter model that can code autonomously for 10+ days
items.idea: Open weights are coming, with a smaller Qwen3.8-27B version dropping next week — a Chinese lab shipping a 2.4T-parameter frontier model with open weights is a direct data point on how fast the US-China model gap is (or isn't) closing.
items.angle: 10+ days of autonomous coding endurance is a different capability axis than benchmark scores — an agents/reliability claim, not a raw-intelligence claim — worth tracking against Anthropic/OpenAI's own long-horizon-agent roadmaps.
items.tweetA: 2.4 trillion parameters, open weights, 10+ days of autonomous coding. Alibaba just shipped a capability the frontier labs talk about as a 2027 milestone — and they're giving the weights away.
items.tweetB: The AI race metric everyone tracks is benchmark scores. The one that actually matters for enterprise adoption is 'how long can it run unsupervised before it breaks.' Qwen just claimed 10+ days. That's the number to interrogate, not the parameter count.

items.title: BitGo's CEO dared Anthropic's Claude to hack a wallet holding 100 BTC — to push back on AI hacking-risk claims
items.idea: The challenge is a live, public test of frontier-model offensive-security capability against a real multi-million-dollar bounty, set up specifically to counter growing claims that AI models are becoming dangerous at wallet-draining and exploit development.
items.angle: Whichever way this resolves becomes a citable data point in the AI-safety-for-crypto debate — a clean pass for Claude undercuts one of the more concrete 'AI is already dangerous' claims currently circulating in security circles.
items.tweetA: A public ~$6M bounty to see if Claude can crack a Bitcoin wallet isn't a stunt, it's the closest thing to a controlled experiment we'll get on 'can frontier AI already drain a wallet today.' Whoever's citing AI hacking risk in vague terms should have to point to this result.
items.tweetB: Notice the frame: BitGo isn't asking 'can AI ever hack a wallet,' it's asking 'can it hack one right now, with no head start.' That's a much narrower and more falsifiable claim than the doom threads assume.

items.title: Aztec Foundation just laid off 55% of its workforce and split into two entities
items.idea: The privacy/ZK-rollup project cut 18 employees and restructured into Aztec Labs plus a separate foundation — a concrete data point on funding conditions for zero-knowledge infrastructure projects that raised heavily during the 2021-22 privacy-tech wave.
items.angle: A 55% cut at a well-funded ZK project is a harder signal on privacy-infra funding conditions than any VC survey — worth checking whether other ZK-rollup teams show similar strain.
items.tweetA: 55% layoffs at a ZK-privacy project that was one of the best-funded names in the category two years ago. The zero-knowledge infrastructure bet hasn't died, but the runway math clearly stopped working.
items.tweetB: Everyone's tracking AI layoffs as a bubble signal. Nobody's tracking that crypto infrastructure — specifically the privacy/ZK corner — just quietly cut more than half its headcount in the same news cycle.

items.title: Goldman: Brent's fair value is ~$80, meaning the market barely has any Middle East risk premium priced in
items.idea: Goldman's fair-value model (OECD inventories, demand estimates, long-term Brent anchor) puts Brent at roughly $80 even as physical flows out of the Persian Gulf and Red Sea are deteriorating sharply and global visible inventories have drawn heavily over the past two weeks.
items.angle: This directly contradicts this morning's 'oil down 4% on Hormuz deal talk' headline — the physical market is tightening while futures price calm, exactly the setup where a single failed diplomacy headline causes a violent repricing, not a gradual one.
items.tweetA: Futures say the Hormuz risk is basically priced out. Physical flows out of the Persian Gulf say the opposite — inventories drawing hard for two straight weeks. When paper and physical disagree this much, physical usually wins, and it wins fast.
items.tweetB: Goldman's own fair value for Brent is $80. Spot is trading well below that on 'deal' headlines. If the deal doesn't materialize, this isn't a slow grind back up — it's a gap, because nobody's holding the risk premium that should be there right now. $USO

items.title: Maxwell Meyer's Frontier-vs-Core framework: DOGE failed for lack of falsifiability, not lack of intent
items.idea: Meyer's thesis is that healthy civilizations balance a 'frontier' (falsifiable, competitive, experimental) against a 'core' (bureaucratic, stabilizing) — he argues Washington DC's wealth concentration signals America has drifted too far toward an unfalsifiable core, where government programs have no natural churn because they're never forced to compete for survival.
items.angle: A useful lens for reading Gebbia/DOGE-style government-efficiency pushes: they only work when the underlying claim is falsifiable (a website either works or doesn't), and fail wherever the objection is political rather than empirical.
items.tweetA: DC suburbs are now the wealthiest place on earth. Meyer's point: that's not a corruption story, it's a falsifiability story — bureaucracies grow forever when nothing forces them to prove they still work. Silicon Valley grows because the market does that pruning automatically.
items.tweetB: The DOGE critics weren't wrong that cuts would get attacked. They were wrong about why: it wasn't the partisanship, it was that most government spending has no falsifiable test of whether it's working. You can't A/B test your way out of that fight.

items.title: OpenAI's Astra just solved 10 outstanding problems in math and theoretical CS — and a leading skeptic conceded the bet
items.idea: University of Toronto's Daniel Litt, previously one of the most prominent skeptics of AI's math-research potential, now writes he no longer believes there's any important type of math AI won't soon be able to do — 'a matter of not too much time' — while some mathematicians are reacting with what one calls a 'profound spiritual crisis.'
items.angle: The emotional reaction is itself a leading indicator worth watching across other credentialed-expertise professions as capability crosses the same threshold — math is just first because proofs are the most legible thing to verify.
items.tweetA: A frontier-math skeptic just conceded his own bet: AI will do essentially all of pure math, 'a matter of not too much time.' A skeptic conceding under evidence is a stronger signal than any benchmark headline this year.
items.tweetB: The mathematician despair here isn't really about job loss — most working mathematicians aren't paid much regardless. It's about status and meaning. Every credentialed profession hits this exact emotional cliff eventually; math just got there first because proofs are the easiest thing to verify.
